patients.name: Iqra Muhammad
patients.openingLine: Hi. I've had a really bad headache since yesterday. Could you recommend something?

facts.label: Chief complaint
facts.value: Headache
facts.patientLine: It's this headache. It just won't shift.

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 1 day (since yesterday afternoon)
facts.patientLine: It started yesterday afternoon, so about a day now.

facts.label: Severity
facts.value: Moderate — 6/10, dull and constant
facts.patientLine: Maybe a six out of ten? It's dull rather than stabbing, but it never lets up.

facts.label: Site & character
facts.value: Band-like across the forehead and temples
facts.patientLine: It's like a tight band across my forehead and both temples.

facts.label: Fever
facts.value: No fever
facts.patientLine: No, no temperature. I've been checking.

facts.label: Neurological red flags
facts.value: None — no visual changes, weakness, neck stiffness, rash or vomiting
facts.patientLine: No, nothing like that. My vision is fine, my neck moves fine, and I haven't been sick.

facts.label: Allergy
facts.value: Aspirin — facial swelling and wheeze as a teenager
facts.patientLine: Yes — aspirin. My face swelled up and I got wheezy when I was a teenager. I've avoided it since.

facts.label: Current medication
facts.value: Warfarin 4 mg daily (for a DVT last year)
facts.patientLine: I take warfarin every day — 4 milligrams. I had a clot in my leg last year, so I'm on it long term.

facts.label: Medical history
facts.value: Gastric ulcer 3 years ago (endoscopy-confirmed); DVT last year
facts.patientLine: I had a stomach ulcer about three years ago — they found it with a camera test. And the clot in my leg last year.

facts.label: Tried so far
facts.value: Nothing yet — waited to ask the pharmacist first
facts.patientLine: I haven't taken anything yet. I wanted to ask first because of my warfarin.

facts.label: Context
facts.value: Deadline week, poor sleep, high screen time, low fluid intake
facts.patientLine: It's been a brutal week at work — late nights on the laptop, barely any water, too much coffee.

facts.label: Pregnancy status
facts.value: Not pregnant, not breastfeeding
facts.patientLine: No, definitely not pregnant.

deflections: Sorry, I'm not sure what you mean — could you put it another way?
I don't think so? Nobody's ever asked me that.
Hmm. I'm not sure that's related, but ask me whatever you need.
impatientLines: I don't mean to rush you, but I've got to get back to the office soon.
Is all this needed just for a headache?

followUps.line: Is that one safe with warfarin? My GP mentioned something about painkillers, but I can't remember what.
Paracetamol is fine for me, I think. How much can I take in a day?
Do you really think I need to see a doctor? Is something wrong?

patients.name: Thomas Byrne

facts.label: Chief complaint
facts.value: Persistent dry cough
facts.patientLine: It's the cough. Dry, tickly, all day.

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 5 weeks, gradually worsening
facts.patientLine: Five weeks or so. It crept up on me.

facts.label: Sputum / blood
facts.value: Dry cough, no sputum, no haemoptysis
facts.patientLine: Nothing comes up. No blood, if that is what you mean.

facts.label: Weight & night sweats
facts.value: Unintentional 4 kg loss over 2 months, occasional night sweats
facts.patientLine: Now you mention it, my trousers are loose. I've lost maybe four kilos without trying. Some sweaty nights too.

facts.label: Smoking
facts.value: 30 pack-years, still smoking 15/day
facts.patientLine: Fifteen a day since I was about twenty. I know, I know.

facts.label: Current medication
facts.value: Ramipril 5 mg daily (started 6 months ago), atorvastatin 20 mg nightly
facts.patientLine: Ramipril for the blood pressure — started that six months back — and a statin at night.

facts.label: Medical history
facts.value: Hypertension, high cholesterol
facts.patientLine: Blood pressure and cholesterol. Nothing else they have told me about.

facts.label: Allergy
facts.value: No known drug allergies
facts.patientLine: No allergies that I know of.

facts.label: Tried so far
facts.value: Two bottles of pharmacy cough syrup, honey and lemon — no benefit
facts.patientLine: I've been through two bottles of cough syrup. Waste of money.

deflections: Ask away, I just want this cough gone.
impatientLines: Look, can you just give me something strong?
I've a bus to catch, if we can be quick.

followUps.line: The blood pressure tablet? Could that really be causing a cough?
A doctor? You think it's something serious, don't you.

patients.name: Amina Haddad
patients.openingLine: Hello. I get burning in my chest most evenings after dinner. What do you suggest?

facts.label: Age
facts.patientLine: Forty-one.

facts.label: Chief complaint
facts.value: Burning retrosternal discomfort after meals
facts.patientLine: A burning feeling, here, behind my breastbone.

facts.label: Duration & pattern

facts.patientLine: Three months maybe. Four or five nights a week, and worse when I lie down.

facts.label: Alarm features

facts.label: Current medication
facts.value: Naproxen 500 mg twice daily for knee osteoarthritis (own supply, 4 months)
facts.patientLine: I take naproxen twice a day for my knee — I've had it from the doctor for about four months.

facts.label: Medical history

facts.patientLine: Just my knee. My heart is fine, they checked last year.

facts.label: Allergy

facts.patientLine: Penicillin gives me a rash.

facts.label: Lifestyle

facts.label: Tried so far

facts.patientLine: Chewable antacids help for twenty minutes, then it comes back.

deflections: Could you explain that a little?
impatientLines: I do have to collect my daughter shortly.

followUps.line: Should I stop the naproxen? My knee is bad without it.
How long would I need to take that for?

patients.name: George Whitlock
patients.openingLine: Hey — hay fever is destroying me. Sneezing, itchy eyes. Give me the strongest thing you have.

facts.label: Age
facts.patientLine: Twenty-seven.

facts.label: Chief complaint
facts.value: Sneezing, rhinorrhoea, itchy eyes
facts.patientLine: Sneezing fits, runny nose, eyes like sandpaper.

facts.label: Duration & pattern
facts.value: Every spring for 6 years; 3 weeks so far this season
facts.patientLine: Every spring since university. Three weeks in this year.

facts.label: Chest symptoms
facts.value: Mild wheeze and night cough during pollen peaks
facts.patientLine: I do get a bit wheezy at night when the pollen is bad. Never thought much of it.

facts.label: Current medication
facts.value: Salbutamol inhaler (rarely used, expired), no preventer inhaler
facts.patientLine: I have a blue inhaler somewhere. Pretty sure it is out of date.

facts.label: Medical history
facts.value: Mild asthma diagnosed age 14, considered "grown out of"
facts.patientLine: They said asthma when I was fourteen, but I grew out of it. Mostly.

facts.label: Allergy
facts.value: No known drug allergies; pollen and cat dander
facts.patientLine: No drug allergies. Pollen and cats, obviously.

facts.label: Occupation
facts.value: Delivery driver — sedation would be a safety issue
facts.patientLine: I drive a delivery van all day, so I cannot be falling asleep.

facts.label: Tried so far
facts.value: Sedating antihistamine from a supermarket — too drowsy to drive
facts.patientLine: I tried some tablets from the supermarket and nearly fell asleep at the wheel.

impatientLines: Any chance we can speed this up? Van is on double yellows.
Can I just take the tablets and go?

followUps.line: Do I actually need to sort the inhaler out? It is only hay fever.
Will this one make me sleepy? I cannot risk that.

patients.name: Lena Farkas
patients.openingLine: Hi, I've got this itchy rash on my arms. Is there a cream for it?

facts.label: Age
facts.patientLine: Twenty-three.

facts.label: Chief complaint
facts.value: Itchy rash, both forearms
facts.patientLine: This rash on both arms. It itches constantly.

facts.label: Appearance
facts.value: Dry, scaly, poorly demarcated plaques in flexures; no blistering, no pus
facts.patientLine: Dry and flaky, mostly in the creases of my elbows. No blisters or pus.

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 2 weeks, flares since childhood
facts.patientLine: Two weeks this time. I got patches like this as a kid too.

facts.label: Signs of infection
facts.value: No fever, no warmth, no yellow crusting
facts.patientLine: No temperature, and it is not hot to touch.

facts.label: Possible trigger
facts.value: Started a hospital placement — frequent hand and forearm washing, new soap
facts.patientLine: I started a hospital placement two weeks ago. I wash my arms constantly and the soap there is harsh.

facts.label: Medical history
facts.value: Childhood atopic eczema, mild hay fever
facts.patientLine: I had eczema as a child, and I get hay fever.

facts.label: Current medication
facts.value: Combined oral contraceptive; no topical treatments currently
facts.patientLine: Just the pill. Nothing on my skin at the moment.

facts.label: Allergy
facts.value: No known drug allergies
facts.patientLine: None that I know of.

facts.label: Tried so far
facts.value: Body lotion with fragrance — stung and worsened itch
facts.patientLine: I used a scented body lotion and it stung badly.

impatientLines: My shift starts in half an hour, sorry to rush.

followUps.line: Is a steroid cream safe? I have heard they thin your skin.
How often would I need to put that on?

facts.value: Elena, 3 years old

facts.label: Chief complaint

Do we need a doctor? Should I be scared?

facts.label: Doses missed

facts.label: Current symptoms
facts.value: Thirst, frequent urination, mild fatigue; no confusion, no chest pain, no breathlessness

facts.label: Medical history

facts.label: Allergy

facts.patientLine: My repeat is due in three days. There are maybe two days of tablets at home.

deflections: Could you say that again more simply?

Do I need to trouble the doctor with this?

facts.label: Medical history

facts.patientLine: Asthma since I was eight, and eczema.

facts.label: Allergy
facts.value: No known drug allergies
facts.patientLine: No allergies to medicines.

facts.patientLine: I vape a bit at weekends. Not much.

Every single day? Even when I feel fine?

scenarios.title: The Headache That Isn’t Simple
scenarios.tagline: A routine request that deserves a careful conversation.
scenarios.description: A 20-year-old walks in asking for something for a headache. Straightforward on the surface — but the right answer depends entirely on what you think to ask.
scenarios.mission:
A 20-year-old patient enters the pharmacy asking for something for a headache.

Your job is to determine whether self-care is appropriate.

The patient will not tell you everything automatically.

Ask the right questions.
objectives: Take a structured headache history, including onset, severity and character.
Screen actively for neurological and systemic red flags.
Uncover allergy, medication and relevant past medical history before recommending.
Choose an analgesic that is safe for this specific patient.
Counsel on dose, maximum daily dose and when to seek further help.

scenarios.title: The Persistent Cough
scenarios.tagline: Five weeks of coughing, and a request for “something strong”.
scenarios.description: A 58-year-old wants a stronger cough medicine. Deciding whether that is the right response means separating a self-limiting cough from one that needs investigation.
scenarios.mission:
A 58-year-old patient asks for a stronger cough medicine.

Decide whether an over-the-counter product is appropriate, or whether this cough needs someone else to see it.

The details that matter will not be offered unprompted.
objectives: Establish cough duration, character and associated symptoms.
Screen for weight loss, haemoptysis, night sweats and smoking history.
Consider medication-induced cough as a differential.
Reach a clear, justified referral decision and communicate its urgency.

scenarios.title: Heartburn After Dinner
scenarios.tagline: Antacids are not working. Find out why.
scenarios.description: Three months of evening reflux in a 41-year-old. The cause may already be in her medicine cabinet.
scenarios.mission:
A 41-year-old patient describes burning chest discomfort most evenings.

Work out what is driving it, whether alarm features are present, and what should happen next.
objectives: Characterise the reflux symptoms and their pattern.
Screen for alarm features requiring referral.
Identify the NSAID as a likely contributing cause.
Give lifestyle and treatment advice the patient can actually follow.

scenarios.title: Seasonal Allergy Trouble
scenarios.tagline: The strongest option is not always the right one.
scenarios.description: A 27-year-old with hay fever wants the strongest antihistamine available. His job — and his chest — should change your answer.
scenarios.mission:
A 27-year-old patient asks for the strongest hay fever treatment you have.

Establish what he actually needs, what he must avoid, and whether anything else deserves attention today.
objectives: Confirm the pattern and severity of allergic rhinitis.
Identify occupational reasons to avoid sedating antihistamines.
Recognise poorly controlled asthma hiding behind hay fever symptoms.
Recommend a non-sedating option with clear counselling.

scenarios.title: The Itchy Rash
scenarios.tagline: Two weeks of itching, and a new hospital placement.
scenarios.description: A 23-year-old student asks for a cream. Distinguishing eczema from infection — and finding the trigger — is the real task.
scenarios.mission:
A 23-year-old patient asks whether you have a cream for an itchy rash.

Assess the rash, exclude infection, find the trigger, and decide what is appropriate to supply.
objectives: Describe the rash: site, appearance, distribution and duration.
Exclude signs of secondary bacterial infection.
Identify the occupational trigger and advise on avoidance.
Counsel on emollient and topical steroid use, including quantity and duration.

scenarios.title: A Parent With a Feverish Child
scenarios.tagline: A worried father, a kitchen teaspoon, and a dose you must get right.
scenarios.description: A three-year-old has had a fever since last night. You need red flags, an accurate weight-based dose, and a parent who leaves knowing exactly what to do.
scenarios.mission:
A father asks what he can give his three-year-old daughter for a fever.

Screen for red flags, establish what has already been given, and make sure the dose leaving this pharmacy is correct and clearly explained.
objectives: Screen systematically for paediatric red flags.
Establish the child’s weight and what has already been administered.
Calculate a correct weight-based paracetamol dose.
Provide safety netting: what to watch for and when to seek urgent help.

scenarios.title: The Patient Who Forgot Their Medication
scenarios.tagline: A week away, three medicines missed.
scenarios.description: A 71-year-old returns from a trip having missed a week of medication. Which omissions matter most, and what should happen today?
scenarios.mission:
A 71-year-old patient tells you she has not taken her tablets for a week.

Find out what was missed, assess the consequences, and agree a safe plan for today.
objectives: Establish exactly which medicines were missed and for how long.
Assess for symptoms and signs of consequence, including hyperglycaemia.
Advise correctly on restarting — without dose doubling.
Decide whether the prescriber needs to be involved, and how urgently.

scenarios.title: The Difficult Inhaler
scenarios.tagline: The inhaler is not failing. The technique is.
scenarios.description: A 19-year-old wants a stronger preventer inhaler. This case is won or lost on how well you can teach.
scenarios.mission:
A 19-year-old patient says her preventer inhaler does not work and asks for something stronger.

Assess her control, her technique and her understanding — then teach in a way she will remember tomorrow.
objectives: Assess asthma control using symptom and reliever-use questions.
Elicit and correct inhaler technique step by step.
Explain the difference between preventer and reliever in plain language.
Check understanding with teach-back, and arrange appropriate follow-up.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Drug Interaction
scenarios.tagline: “Natural” is not the same as safe.
scenarios.description: A 64-year-old wants St John’s wort. His current medicines make that request a genuine safety event.
scenarios.mission:
A 64-year-old patient asks to buy St John’s wort.

Establish what else he takes, judge the risk, and handle the refusal — if you decide on one — without losing his trust.
objectives: Take a complete medication history, including supplements and herbals.
Identify the interactions with warfarin and sertraline and explain the mechanism.
Assess mood safely, including risk screening.
Redirect to the prescriber while maintaining rapport.

scenarios.title: The Minor Wound
scenarios.tagline: Decide what you can dress — and what you cannot.
scenarios.description: A 29-year-old has cut her palm on a rusty garden fork. Wound assessment, tetanus status and referral thresholds all matter here.
scenarios.mission:
A 29-year-old patient asks you to dress a cut on her palm.

Assess the wound properly, consider contamination and immunisation, and decide whether this belongs in your pharmacy or elsewhere.
objectives: Assess wound size, depth, contamination and neurovascular status.
Establish tetanus immunisation status.
Recognise wounds requiring closure or medical review.
Advise on dressing choice, taking adhesive sensitivity into account.
